• Common name: Swordtail
  • Scientific name: Xiphophorus helleri
  • Adult size: 3-4 inches (about 8-10 cm)
  • Life expectancy: 3-5 years
  • Family: Poeciliidae
  • Origin: Mexico and Central America
  • Social: Peaceful
  • Tank level: Top, mid-dweller
  • Minimum tank size: 20 gallons (about 75 litres)
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Breeding: Livebearer
  • Care: Easy
  • pH 7.0-8.5
  • Hardness: 12-30 dGH
  • Temperature: 18 to 28 °C (64 to 82 °F)

Some websites and pet stores offer "specialty" varieties that are not found anywhere else. Keep in mind that many of these unique breeds are generated through several generations of inbreeding. Although their external appearances may be very distinctive, they may also have internal issues with limited immune function and longevity.

Swordtails are named for the male's elongated ventral aspect of the tail fin, creating a "sword"-like appearance. They are bred in a wide variety of colorations. Among the varieties of swordtails, you can expect vibrant reds, yellows and blacks with a mix of bars and stripes. There are also longfin varieties of swordtails that have elongated dorsal, pectoral and tail fins.

The specimens offered are bred ones from Southeast Asia.

The subspecies Xiphophorus hellerii guentheri has been described from Guatemala. In Germany spotted swordtails are usually called "guentheri". The "Golden Stream" does not fit what is thought of as a guentheri, but the name has been widely accepted in the livebearer community, so it should not be changed without pressing need. It is far more important that such animals are bred in pure strains. Only then will it be possible in the future to study the behaviour and genetics of wild fish. There already exist enough artificial sports and crosses.

Swordtail fish have been a vibrant component of the aquarium hobbyist community for many years. Originating from Mexico and Central America, the Swordtail has been bred in captivity for countless generations. There are many varieties widely available to the aquarium community, including the naturally colored green swordtail, as well as neon, pineapple, painted, marigold wag, red wag and hi fin lyretail.

This unusual Green Swordtail originates from the surroundings of the Golden Stream preserve in Belize. The preserve covers an area of about 61 km² and contains a large number of rare and endangered species.

Swordtails do well in many different aquarium setups. These easygoing fish are good for beginners and a colorful addition to any community tank. They are active fish, so make sure there are not too many decorative items in their way. The best combination is to keep décor and plants to the lower half to two-thirds of the tank and leave the top of the tank open for active swimming.

Swordtails are omnivores that enjoy a varied diet. Depending on the water temperature, you may need to feed your fish 2-3 times per day. Many tropical fish like to forage throughout the day, so fewer feedings are not ideal. Swordtails do well on most community micropelleted diets, and also enjoy occasional frozen and freeze-dried treats.

Swordtails do best living in a group, so plan on at least 4-5 individuals per aquarium. You can mix different varieties together, but be ready for a swarm of baby swordtails if you mix males and females. Some potential tankmates include Neon Tetras, Coolie Loach or Corydoras.

Male swordtails may take up territory and become aggressive towards other fish. Be sure to have plenty of room for all your swordtails, despite their small size. It may help to add fake or live plants to give your fish more hiding areas.

Males have the characteristic "sword" on the ventral aspect of the tail. Females have a rounded tail edge and tend to have thicker bodies, from carrying live fry. The anal fin is also pointed in males and fan-shaped in females. This can be used to determine sex in young fish before the males develop their long sword.

One of the peculiarities of the "Golden Stream" is that a natural polymorphism still exists in males. From the same brood one can obtain small, tiny, often very colourful males and real bulls with about double the body mass of their small conspecifics. These so-called early and late males appear initially in any swordtail population, but in domesticated strains breeders often eliminate the small early males, so only large, late males exist.

The males often exhibit dark vertical stripes on the shoulder.

Livebearers such as swordtails can easily overpopulate an aquarium. Many beginners are not aware of the swordtail's livebearing abilities and are surprised by a swarm of babies. Females may already be pregnant when acquired, and even one pregnant swordtail can cause a sudden population explosion.

Swordtails can mature as early as 3 months old and give birth to up to 50 fry per spawning. If you don't want more babies, separate males from females before they reach reproductive maturity.

Over several generations, you may note an increase in fry deaths, or your fish may not live as long. If you continue to breed the same population, you can expect health issues resulting from inbreeding. The best fix is adding genetic diversity by purchasing new fish or trading with another hobbyist. Unless you know the health history of new fish, it is always recommended to quarantine them before adding them to your aquarium.

The "Golden Stream" is a wonderful wild type of swordtail that can be recommended to hobbyists interested in studies of behaviour and genetics, but a hobbyist who simply enjoys beautiful fish will also make a good choice.
